articles.title: NEMA Launches Innovative Aerospace Technology from Rochdale
articles.excerpt: NEMA, a Rochdale-based aerospace firm, is pioneering next-generation technology to support the aviation sector's transition to more sustainable aircraft. Established in 1954, the company continues to innovate in precision engineering.
articles.content_html:
NEMA, a Rochdale-based aerospace and defence company, is set to lead the way in advanced aerospace technology. Established in 1954 as The Nordale Spring Company, NEMA has evolved significantly over the decades, changing its name in 2003 to Nordale Electro-Mechanical Actuation. The firm has built a reputation for designing and manufacturing precision-engineered motors, generators, and components, and is now recognised as one of the UK's leading specialists in high-performance aerospace components.

Operating from the Chichester Business Centre, NEMA has been instrumental in supporting the global aerospace and defence sectors. The company offers a comprehensive range of engineering solutions, from concept development and prototyping to production and aftermarket support. This full-service approach enables NEMA to assist clients in bringing advanced aerospace technologies into service with confidence.

A key focus for NEMA is the development of electrification technologies that facilitate the aviation sector's shift towards more-electric and hybrid-electric aircraft. These innovations are designed to improve efficiency, reduce weight, enhance reliability, and lower the environmental impact of aviation operations.

The Rochdale Development Agency has supported NEMA throughout its journey, helping to position the company as a significant player in the advanced manufacturing landscape. As NEMA continues to innovate, it is expected to contribute further to the local economy and the aerospace industry as a whole.

articles.title: Long Delays on M62 Eastbound Near Rochdale Due to Breakdown
articles.excerpt: Drivers on the M62 eastbound near Rochdale are facing significant delays this afternoon, with queues stretching five miles following a breakdown between junctions 20 and 21.
articles.content_html:
Drivers on the M62 eastbound near Rochdale are experiencing long delays this afternoon, September 14, due to a breakdown that has closed one lane of traffic. The incident occurred between junctions 20 and 21, resulting in queues extending five miles, according to National Highways.

Traffic Officers and recovery services are currently on the scene, working to clear the broken down vehicle. As a result of the incident, drivers are facing delays of approximately 35 minutes on approach to the affected area, with congestion reported to be tailing back past junction 19 at Heywood.

Motorists are advised to plan their journeys accordingly, as the delays are likely to persist until the vehicle is removed and the lane is reopened. The situation is being monitored by National Highways.

This incident underscores the importance of vehicle maintenance for drivers using the M62, particularly during peak travel times. Those travelling in the area should remain alert and consider alternative routes if possible.

articles.title: Rochdale Procurement 360 Summit to Help Local Businesses Secure Public-Sector Contracts
articles.excerpt: The Rochdale Procurement 360 Summit, organised by Rochdale Development Agency, will take place on October 7 at Crown Oil Arena, aiming to help local businesses navigate public sector procurement.
articles.content_html:
An event aimed at assisting businesses in Rochdale to secure public sector contracts is scheduled for Wednesday, October 7. The Rochdale Procurement 360 Summit will be held at the Crown Oil Arena, home of Rochdale AFC.

Organised by the Rochdale Development Agency (RDA), the summit will feature keynote presentations, expert panel discussions, and networking opportunities. Attendees will gain insights into public sector procurement processes, what buyers seek in successful bids, and how to leverage social value to enhance their proposals.

The RDA stated that billions of pounds are spent annually through public sector procurement. The summit aims to connect local businesses with public sector organisations and procurement professionals, fostering opportunities that can contribute to the borough's economic growth and job creation. This initiative supports Rochdale’s ambition to increase the value of public sector contracts secured by local businesses, ultimately helping to create jobs and improve productivity.

The event is designed for both established suppliers and those looking to enter the public sector market. STAR Procurement will also participate in a panel discussion, providing practical insights and answering questions related to procurement and bidding processes.

articles.title: Middleton Residents Call for Reconsideration of Parking Restrictions on Grimshaw Lane
articles.excerpt: Residents on Grimshaw Lane in Middleton are urging local councillors to rethink proposed parking restrictions aimed at improving safety and traffic flow. The plans will be discussed at the Middleton Township Committee meeting on 14 September 2026.
articles.content_html:
Residents on Grimshaw Lane in Middleton are urging local councillors to reconsider proposed parking restrictions that could significantly affect parking outside their homes. The Middleton Township Committee is set to discuss objections to these plans during its meeting on Thursday, 14 September 2026.

The proposed restrictions come in response to ongoing issues with speeding, serious accidents—including a fatality—and inconsiderate parking that has disrupted bus services in the area. A report from Rochdale Council's Highways department highlights that the north-western section of Grimshaw Lane, between Greengate and Townley Street, has been identified as a location with poor bus service reliability due to congestion and obstructive parking.

To address these concerns, the council's proposal includes the installation of new footway build-outs to narrow pedestrian crossing widths at several junctions, as well as the addition of three new pedestrian refuge islands to facilitate safer crossings. Furthermore, the plans involve extending bus stop bays and introducing double yellow lines along much of the northern side of Grimshaw Lane, particularly from Saxon Street to Sedgley Street, to ensure the safe passage of vehicles, including refuse collection and HGVs servicing local businesses.

The outcome of the committee meeting will determine whether the proposed parking restrictions will be implemented or if further adjustments will be made to accommodate residents' concerns. Local residents are encouraged to attend the meeting to voice their opinions on the matter.

articles.excerpt: The lift at Failsworth tram stop is currently out of service, affecting access for passengers. Those requiring step-free access are advised to travel to Hollinwood.
articles.content_html:
The lift at Failsworth tram stop, which services the platform heading to Rochdale, is out of service due to replacement works. This situation has been in effect since 2:47pm on Sunday, 13 September 2026, and will continue until further notice.

As a result of the lift being out of service, there is currently no step-free access available at this stop. Passengers who require step-free access are advised to make their way to Hollinwood tram stop to connect to services.

Customers needing assistance with journey planning are encouraged to contact the Metrolink customer service centre at 0161 244 1000. The lines are open from 7am to 8pm on weekdays and from 8am to 8pm on weekends and Bank Holidays.

Further updates regarding the lift service will be provided as they become available. Passengers are advised to check the Bee Network live travel alerts for the latest information.

articles.title: Maggie’s Oldham Announces Culture Crawl Fundraiser from Oldham to Rochdale
articles.excerpt: The Culture Crawl will raise funds for Maggie’s Oldham, supporting people affected by cancer, as it takes participants on a 10k walk from Oldham to Rochdale Town Hall.
articles.content_html:
Maggie’s Oldham is inviting locals to participate in its annual Culture Crawl on Saturday, September 26, which aims to raise funds for individuals living with cancer and their families. This year, the 10-kilometre walk will start in Oldham and finish at the iconic Rochdale Town Hall, marking the first time the event will include Rochdale in its route.

Participants will have the opportunity to explore local history, culture, and community spirit along the way. The event promises a day filled with entertainment, food, and opportunities to engage with the unique stories of the two boroughs. Registration will begin at 12pm at The Loom, where walkers will gather before setting off towards Rochdale.

Sharon Furlong, whose husband has received support from Maggie’s Oldham during his cancer journey, expressed the significance of the event, stating, "Taking part in Maggie’s Culture Crawl this year means so much to me." Every penny raised will go directly towards supporting those affected by cancer, ensuring that Maggie’s can continue to provide vital services.

The Culture Crawl not only serves as a fundraising initiative but also aims to strengthen community ties between Oldham and Rochdale, making it a memorable day for individuals, families, and teams alike. Participants are encouraged to register early to secure their place in this meaningful event.

articles.title: Are there really fairies in Healey Dell?
articles.excerpt: The Fairies’ Chapel is a real and much‑loved spot in Healey Dell — but its supernatural stories belong to the region’s folklore, not its archives.
articles.summary: The Fairies’ Chapel is a real and much‑loved spot in Healey Dell — but its supernatural stories belong to the region’s folklore, not its archives.
articles.body:
Ask any walker who’s slipped down the steep steps to the riverside at Healey Dell and you’ll get the same mixture of delight and bemusement: a narrow rocky cleft that looks, if you squint, a little like a chapel, and a name — the Fairies’ Chapel — that invites imagination. The place is part of a managed nature reserve with a heritage centre and tea rooms; its landscape is the product of geology, industry and decades of storytelling. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale))

The feature people call the Fairies’ Chapel sits in a gorge known locally as “the Thrutch”, where the River Spodden squeezes through rock to make falls and pools. Erosion has hollowed niches and smooth grooves that earlier visitors likened to benches and a pulpit carved in stone — an entirely natural effect of the water working the sandstone over centuries. Local guides and the Healey Dell Heritage Centre explain the physical origin of the name alongside the site’s visitor attractions for families. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/things-to-do/the-fairies-chapel/))

The documented history of the Dell is straightforward and well recorded. The valley contains the remains of water‑powered mills and reservoirs; a disused nineteenth‑century railway line now forms a trail; and the high viaduct that dominates the view is a Grade II listed structure on the National Heritage List for England. These are matters of record: industrial archaeology, recorded listing details and the council’s nature‑reserve management form the verifiable backbone of Healey Dell’s story. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1317784))

The fairy stories are a different matter. The best‑known written version of the Fairies’ Chapel tale appears in John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire (1829–31), a collection of local romances and folk narratives that includes a dramatic account involving a miller, Lady Eleanor (a Byron), enchanted gatherings and a Fairy Queen. Roby’s work preserves how nineteenth‑century readers and storytellers cast the Dell, but it is a literary record of folklore rather than archival evidence of historical events. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/25256/pg25256-images.html))

Folklore collectors and later guides have mixed motifs — fairies, witches, a Fairy King, even a Robin Hood‑like figure in some retellings — so you will find several versions in print and on local heritage pages. These stories are culturally valuable: they tell us how people have related to the landscape, explained strange rock shapes and given meaning to the place. But none of the dramatic supernatural claims in the tales (for example, fairies turning witches to stone or prophetic fairy queens) are backed by independent documentary records; they survive in oral tradition and literary retelling. If a claim cannot be verified in parish records, legal documents or contemporary reports, it should be treated as folklore. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/25256/pg25256-images.html))

One concrete historical note helps show how the Dell changed: nineteenth‑century guides and more recent heritage material point to a major storm and flood on 4 July 1838 that altered sections of the Spodden and the features visitors once saw. Floods and later human activity mean the rocks and cavities admired by earlier writers are not exactly as they were, which helps explain differences between story and present‑day topography. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/history/Fairies-Chapel-final.pdf))

So: are there fairies in Healey Dell? If you mean tiny supernatural beings recorded by contemporary evidence — no. If you mean a place where natural rock formations, industrial remnants and 150‑plus years of storytelling meet and feed the imagination — very much yes. The Fairies’ Chapel is best enjoyed on two levels: look closely at the geology and the listed structures that are historically verifiable, and then listen to the old tales (Roby and later local guides are the main published sources) as a living part of local culture. Both make Healey Dell worth a visit. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale))

Aden Flint has expressed optimism following Rochdale AFC's recent 1-1 draw against Walsall on Saturday, September 12, 2026. The defender stated that the point gained from the match is something the team can build upon as they seek to enhance their performance in the league.

Flint highlighted the importance of the result, suggesting it provides a platform for the team to develop and improve in upcoming fixtures. He emphasised the need for the squad to learn from their experiences and focus on consistency moving forward.

Looking ahead, Flint and his teammates are determined to translate this draw into a series of positive results, aiming to climb the league table as the season progresses.

articles.title: Ian Watson Praises Team's Mentality After Draw Against Walsall
articles.excerpt: Rochdale's manager Ian Watson praised his team's resilience after they held Walsall to a goalless draw in League Two, marking a crucial point following a challenging start to the season.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale AFC managed to secure a valuable point in a 0-0 draw against Walsall at the Bescot Stadium on Saturday, 12 September 2026. The match came just days after manager Ian Watson received a vote of confidence from the club following a difficult start to the League Two season, with only one win from their first five matches since promotion from the National League under previous manager Jimmy McNulty.

Despite Walsall dominating possession with 70% and registering 24 shots, Rochdale's defence held firm, limiting clear opportunities for the home side. Notably, Baba Adeeko came close to scoring for Rochdale, hitting the crossbar with a shot in the first half. Watson highlighted the team's fighting spirit, stating, "Sometimes you need to set up a little bit differently away from home... we spoke about the mentality we would need, being warriors and stopping the ball going in our net."

Walsall's pressure intensified throughout the match, with Nils Ramming making crucial saves, including a double stop from close-range efforts. However, despite their efforts, Walsall could not find the back of the net, marking their fourth goalless draw in eight games this season. Walsall manager Lee Grant expressed mixed emotions, feeling proud of his team's performance but disappointed at dropping points at home.

The draw leaves Rochdale with a point that could prove vital as they look to build momentum in the league. The team will aim to improve their performance in upcoming fixtures as they seek to climb the League Two table. Fans will be hoping that this result can serve as a turning point for the squad as they adapt to the challenges of the new season.

articles.title: Mother Hubbard Opens in Middleton, Boosting Local Fish and Chip Trade
articles.excerpt: Mother Hubbard has opened a new branch in Middleton Shopping Centre, offering 45p fish and chips to the first 1,000 customers, boosting local fish and chip sales including at the nearby Middleton Fish Bar.
articles.content_html:
A new fish and chip shop, Mother Hubbard, opened its doors in Middleton Shopping Centre on Saturday, 12 September 2026, offering a special promotion of 45p fish and chips for the first 1,000 customers. This opening drew significant crowds, with queues stretching back to the bus station as locals flocked to sample the menu.

Among the first customers was Colin Thompson, who praised the quality of the food and the hard work of the staff on social media. Other patrons echoed his sentiments, expressing excitement about the new addition to the local dining scene. Misa Ila commented on Facebook, stating, "Great venue, good luck to them. The Rochdale one is mint," while Pat Keogh added, "Well done and good luck. Glad Middleton is getting sorted now, it’s about time."

The opening of Mother Hubbard coincided with a busy day for the nearby Middleton Fish Bar, which reported selling out of its stock and closing early at 2.30pm due to high demand. Owners Paul and Caroline High thanked their customers for their support, highlighting the strong community response to both establishments.

The successful launch of Mother Hubbard and the bustling trade at Middleton Fish Bar suggest a growing appetite for fish and chips in the area, which may encourage further investment in local dining options. Residents can expect a vibrant fish and chip scene in Middleton as both businesses continue to serve the community.
